analysis.one_liner: Gives one drug's patent holder ten more years of exclusive rights.
analysis.headline: A bill to extend the patent on the drug Ethiofos by ten years was referred to the House Judiciary Committee in February 1990, drew no cosponsors, and never received a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: H.R. 4129 was a private bill directing the Commerce Department to extend U.S. Patent 3,892,824 — covering the drug Ethiofos (WR2721) and its oral form — for ten years after it expired [S2][S3]. That would have added a decade of legally protected monopoly sales for one product beyond the normal patent term. The bill was introduced on February 27, 1990, referred to the House Judiciary Committee, and died there without action [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the holder of Patent 3,892,824 — the patent owner and any company licensed to sell Ethiofos (WR2721) — would have gained ten additional years of exclusive rights to the drug, with "all the rights pertaining thereto" to the compound, its hydrates, and its salts [S3]. A patent monopoly lets the owner set the price without generic competition, so the extension would have locked in patent-level pricing for a decade longer than the law normally allows. No other company or group is named in the bill; its sole effect is to extend this one patent [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Extends U.S. Patent 3,892,824 for ten years after its normal expiration, giving the owner continued exclusive rights to Ethiofos (WR2721), its oral analogue, and related salts with 'all the rights pertaining thereto' [S3].
Because a patent bars generic copies, the extension would let the patent holder and its licensee keep selling the drug without competition, at monopoly prices, for an extra decade.

analysis.who_pays: Patients who need the drug — the bill covers a medication (Ethiofos/WR2721, a protective agent used alongside cancer treatment) — would pay patent-protected prices for ten additional years, as would insurers and health programs buying it. Generic drug makers would also be barred from selling competing versions during the extension. Anyone paying higher prices for this one drug bears the cost of the monopoly's extra decade.
analysis.who_pays_short: Patients and insurers buying the drug

drawbacks.text: The bill is special-interest legislation: it does not change patent law for anyone else, it simply directs the Commerce Department to add ten years to one named patent (3,892,824), circumventing the standard patent term that applies to every other invention [S3][S2].
An extended patent blocks generic competition for ten more years, so patients and insurers would pay higher prices for the drug than they would once the patent lapsed [S3].
No evidence of a public need for the extension appears in the bill or its official summary — the CRS summary states only that the patent 'shall' be extended [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's entire benefit would flow to a single patent holder: ten extra years of exclusive sales on one drug [S3]. The cost — a decade of patent-protected pricing for patients and health programs, and delayed generic competition — would be spread across the people who use and pay for the drug [S3]. There is no offsetting public benefit anywhere in the bill text or summary; it is a targeted monopoly extension, and its failure was a win for the public.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Judiciary Committee, which never took it up, so it died quietly when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Mike Synar introduced the bill on February 27, 1990, with no cosponsors [S1][S4][S5].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary, the standard first step for patent legislation [S5].
The committee never reported the bill, no committee or floor vote was ever held, and no further action of any kind appears in the record [S5].
The 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991, and the bill lapsed [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Patients and the public, who avoided an extra decade of patent-protected pricing on Ethiofos, and generic drug makers, who could enter once the patent ran its normal course. The patent holder got nothing because the bill died.

for.name: Rep. Mike Synar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill extending Patent 3,892,824 for ten years; no member cosponsored it

against.name: House Judiciary Committee (Chair Jack Brooks)
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over patent bills
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never reported it, held no markup or vote, and let it die

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the Democratic sponsor had no cosponsors of either party, so no partisan split exists in the record [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Ethiofos patent holder and its pharmaceutical licensee
industries.note: The bill would have handed this single patent ten more years of exclusive rights to sell the drug, including its oral form and salt variants [S3]. Its gain — a longer monopoly — is paid for directly by patients in higher prices.
A ten-year extension would have kept competing generic versions of Ethiofos off the market for a decade after the patent's normal end [S3].
Any private patent-extension precedent strengthens the brand-drug model of stretching monopoly terms through Congress rather than the standard patent system, keeping drug prices above generic levels.
